related_questions.question: What are the new guidelines for diabetes?

text_blocks.snippet: The latest American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care for 2025 emphasize personalized approaches to diabetes management, including updated recommendations for screening, medication, and technology use. Key changes include a lower screening age for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, expanded use of GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists, and a greater focus on integrating diabetes technology like CGM.
snippet_highlighted_words: a lower screening age for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, expanded use of GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists, and a greater focus on integrating diabetes technology like CGM

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at the updates:

list.snippet: The recommended age for screening for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes has been lowered from 45 to 35 years old.
All adults with overweight or obesity and at least one risk factor should be screened, including those with a family history of diabetes and physical inactivity.
All women, regardless of risk factors, should be tested for undiagnosed diabetes at pregnancy planning or their first prenatal visit.
Gestational diabetes screening should be performed at 24-28 weeks of gestation for women not previously diagnosed with diabetes.

list.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists
list.snippet: are recommended for individuals with type 2 diabetes and established or high risk for cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, according to the NIDDK.

list.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists
list.snippet: are also recommended for individuals with type 2 diabetes and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).

list.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists
list.snippet: are considered for people with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

list.title: Newer medications
list.snippet: like SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists are recommended for adults with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycemic control despite metformin and lifestyle modifications.
Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM): is recommended for all individuals with type 1 diabetes and those with type 2 diabetes on insulin therapy.
CGM should be considered for adults with type 2 diabetes on glucose-lowering agents other than insulin.
CGM metrics can be used alongside blood glucose monitoring to achieve optimal glycemic goals.
CGM can help achieve glycemic goals (e.g., time in range, time above range) and A1C goals.
Emphasis on individual risk/benefit assessment of pre-diabetes.
Sleep: is highlighted as a central component of diabetes management, equal to eating patterns and physical activity.
Intensive lifestyle behavior change programs: are recommended for all overweight/obese individuals at risk, with specific weight loss goals based on BMI and A1C.
Diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES): is emphasized for all individuals with diabetes.
Behavioral health screenings: should be conducted alongside DSMES assessments.
Remote delivery of DSMES: is recognized and reimbursed.
Social determinants of health: should be considered in DSMES design and delivery.
Guidance on DKA and HHS: in outpatient and inpatient settings.
Screening updates for fear of hypoglycemia, diabetes distress, and anxiety .
Improved approach to diabetes care for older adults .
